description: Georgia's filing deadline for childhood sexual abuse depends on when the abuse happened. O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33.1, the discovery rule, and institutions.
shortAnswer: The law is O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33.1, and the rules now depend on the date of the abuse. Abuse before July 1, 2015: by the survivor’s 23rd birthday. Abuse on or after July 1, 2015: by the 23rd birthday, or within two years of the date the survivor knew, or had reason to know, of the abuse.

sections.heading: The deadline depends on when the abuse happened
sections.shortAnswer: Abuse before July 1, 2015: the lawsuit must be filed by the survivor’s 23rd birthday. Abuse on or after July 1, 2015: by the 23rd birthday, or within two years under the discovery rule.

sections.heading: Abusers and institutions are not treated the same
sections.shortAnswer: If the suit is filed by the 23rd birthday, the survivor must show the entity was negligent. If filed later under the discovery rule, the survivor must show the entity was grossly negligent, knew or should have known, and failed to take remedial action.

sections.heading: Parents have a claim and a clock of their own
sections.shortAnswer: The money for counseling, for hospital stays, and for other medical costs while your child is a minor is usually your claim. Treat it as running on the ordinary clock: two years.

sections.heading: A criminal case and a civil case are different things
sections.shortAnswer: Please report first. Your child’s safety, and the safety of other children, comes before any lawsuit. A civil case can reach the people and institutions who let it happen, and it can pay for the care your child will need.

sections.heading: If your child has just told you
sections.shortAnswer: Believe your child. Get your child away from the person, and report it. Save everything. Do not sign anything from the institution’s lawyer or insurance company before you get advice.

sections.heading: If you are an adult survivor
sections.shortAnswer: Find out which deadline applies to you before you assume it has passed. The date of the abuse, your age, and what you learned and when all matter.

faq.q: How long does a survivor of childhood sexual abuse have to sue in Georgia?
faq.a: For abuse before July 1, 2015, the lawsuit must be filed by the survivor’s 23rd birthday. For abuse on or after July 1, 2015, by the 23rd birthday, or within two years of the date the survivor knew, or had reason to know, of the abuse and that it caused the survivor’s injury.

faq.q: Can a survivor sue a church or school for childhood sexual abuse in Georgia?
faq.a: Section 9-3-33.1 has a separate rule for claims against an entity. If the suit is filed by the 23rd birthday, the survivor must show the entity was negligent. If filed later under the discovery rule, the survivor must show the entity was grossly negligent, knew or should have known, and failed to take remedial action.

faq.q: Should we wait for the police before filing a civil case for child sexual abuse?
faq.a: Please report first. But the two systems do different jobs. A civil case is brought by the survivor, the standard of proof is lower, and it can reach the people and institutions who let it happen.
